Complete PWA Implementation Guide - GurukulamHub
================================================

What is PWA (Progressive Web App)?
-----------------------------------
PWA stands for Progressive Web App. It's a web application that behaves like a native mobile/desktop app with these features:

Key Features:
1. Offline Support - Works without internet connection
2. Installable - Can be installed on device (like an app)
3. Fast Loading - Caches resources for instant loading
4. App-like Experience - Full-screen, no browser UI
5. Push Notifications - Can send notifications (if implemented)
6. Responsive - Works on all devices

How PWA Works:
- Service Worker - A JavaScript file that runs in the background, intercepts network requests, and caches resources
- Manifest - A JSON file that tells the browser how to display the app when installed
- Caching Strategy - Rules for what to cache and when to use cached vs network data


Files Involved in PWA Implementation
======================================

1. next.config.mjs - PWA Configuration
Purpose: Configures the PWA plugin and Workbox settings

What it does:
- Wraps Next.js config with withPWA() plugin
- Generates service worker files automatically
- Configures caching strategies
- Sets up offline fallback page
- Excludes source maps from production

Key Settings:
const pwaConfig = withPWA({
  dest: 'public',              // Where to output service worker files
  disable: false,              // Enable PWA
  register: true,              // Auto-register service worker
  skipWaiting: true,           // Activate new SW immediately
  sw: 'sw.js',                 // Service worker filename
  fallbacks: {
    document: '/offline.html'  // Show this when offline
  },
  workboxOptions: {
    // Caching strategies for different resources
    runtimeCaching: [...]
  }
})

Caching Strategies Used:
- CacheFirst: For static assets (images, fonts) - Use cache first, network as fallback
- NetworkFirst: For pages/API - Try network first, cache as fallback


2. public/manifest.json - App Manifest
Purpose: Defines how the app appears when installed

What it contains:
- App name and description
- Icons (192x192, 512x512)
- Display mode (standalone = no browser UI)
- Theme colors
- Start URL

How it works:
- Browser reads this file
- Shows "Install App" prompt if criteria met
- Creates app icon on home screen
- Sets app metadata

Example:
{
  "name": "GurukulamHub - Indian Knowledge Systems",
  "short_name": "GurukulamHub",
  "start_url": "/",
  "display": "standalone",  // No browser UI
  "icons": [
    { "src": "/icons/icon-192x192.png", "sizes": "192x192" },
    { "src": "/icons/icon-512x512.png", "sizes": "512x512" }
  ]
}


3. public/sw.js - Service Worker (Main File)
Purpose: The core service worker that handles caching and offline functionality

What it does:
- Precaching: Downloads and caches critical files on install
- Runtime Caching: Caches resources as they're requested
- Offline Handling: Serves cached content when offline
- Update Management: Checks for updates and activates new versions

How it's generated:
- Created automatically by @ducanh2912/next-pwa plugin
- Generated during npm run build or npm run dev
- Contains Workbox code + your caching configuration

Key Functions:
// Precaching - Cache these files immediately
self.__WB_MANIFEST = [
  { url: '/offline.html', revision: 'abc123' },
  { url: '/icons/icon-192x192.png', revision: 'xyz789' },
  // ... more files
]

// Runtime Caching - Cache on demand
workbox.routing.registerRoute(
  /\.(?:png|jpg|jpeg|svg|gif)$/,
  new workbox.strategies.CacheFirst()
)

Lifecycle:
1. Install: Downloads precache files
2. Activate: Clears old cache, activates new SW
3. Fetch: Intercepts network requests
4. Update: Checks for new version every 24 hours


4. public/sw.js.map - Source Map (Development Only)
Purpose: Maps minified code back to original source for debugging

What it does:
- Helps debug service worker in browser DevTools
- Shows original file/line numbers in errors
- NOT needed in production - Only for development

Why we remove it:
- Increases file size
- Not needed by end users
- Can cause unnecessary service worker updates
- Security: Exposes source code structure

How we handle it:
- Generated automatically in dev mode
- Removed by remove-sourcemap.js script after build
- Added to .gitignore to prevent git tracking


5. public/workbox-*.js - Workbox Library
Purpose: Google's Workbox library that powers the service worker

What it does:
- Provides caching strategies (CacheFirst, NetworkFirst, etc.)
- Handles cache management
- Manages service worker lifecycle
- Provides precaching functionality

File naming:
- workbox-1e54d6fe.js - Hash in name ensures cache busting
- Hash changes when Workbox version changes
- Browser downloads new version automatically

Why separate file:
- Workbox is large (~50KB)
- Cached separately from your service worker
- Can be shared across multiple service workers
- Updates independently


6. public/workbox-*.js.map - Workbox Source Map
Purpose: Source map for Workbox library (development only)

What it does:
- Same as sw.js.map but for Workbox library
- Helps debug Workbox code
- NOT needed in production

How we handle it:
- Generated in dev mode
- Removed by remove-sourcemap.js script
- Ignored by git


7. public/fallback-development.js - Fallback Script
Purpose: Helper script for development mode service worker

What it does:
- Provides additional functionality in development
- Handles development-specific caching
- May include debugging utilities

Note: This file is auto-generated and may vary based on PWA plugin version.


8. public/offline.html - Offline Fallback Page
Purpose: The page shown when user is offline and page isn't cached

What it does:
- Displays friendly "You're Offline" message
- Shows app icon
- Provides "Retry" button
- Matches app theme (light/dark mode)

How it works:
1. User goes offline
2. Tries to visit a page not in cache
3. Service worker intercepts request
4. Serves offline.html instead
5. User sees offline message

Theme Support:
- Detects app's theme from localStorage
- Supports light/dark mode
- Falls back to system preference

Dynamic Updates:
- Uses content hash for versioning
- Changes to file trigger service worker update
- Ensures users see latest version


9. scripts/remove-sourcemap.js - Post-Build Cleanup
Purpose: Removes source maps after production build

What it does:
1. Finds all .js files in public/ (sw.js, workbox-*.js, fallback-*.js)
2. Removes //# sourceMappingURL=... comments from each file
3. Deletes all .map files from public/ directory
4. Logs what was cleaned

Why needed:
- Source maps are for development only
- They increase file size
- They can trigger unnecessary service worker updates
- Not needed in production

When it runs:
- Automatically after npm run build
- Part of build process: "build": "next build && node scripts/remove-sourcemap.js"

Example Output:
Cleaning source maps for production...

Removed source map reference from sw.js
Removed source map reference from workbox-1e54d6fe.js
Deleted sw.js.map
Deleted workbox-1e54d6fe.js.map

Source map cleanup completed for production!


10. src/middleware.js - Middleware Configuration
Purpose: Ensures PWA files are served correctly

What it does:
- Skips middleware processing for PWA files
- Allows service worker, manifest, and offline.html to be served directly
- Prevents authentication/routing logic from interfering with PWA

Key Code:
// Skip middleware for PWA files
if (
  pathname === '/manifest.json' ||
  pathname === '/sw.js' ||
  pathname === '/offline.html' ||
  pathname.startsWith('/workbox-') ||
  pathname.startsWith('/fallback-')
) {
  return NextResponse.next() // Serve directly, no middleware processing
}

Why needed:
- Service worker must be served from root domain
- Must not be redirected or modified
- Must have correct MIME type
- Must be accessible without authentication


11. src/components/PWARegistration.jsx - Client-Side Registration
Purpose: Registers service worker and provides debugging info

What it does:
- Checks if service worker is supported
- Logs registration status to console
- Monitors service worker updates
- Checks if app is installable
- Detects if app is running in standalone mode

How it works:
- Runs on client-side only ('use client')
- Uses useEffect to run once on mount
- Checks navigator.serviceWorker API
- Provides console logs for debugging

Console Output:
PWA: Service Worker API is available
PWA: Service Worker is already registered
PWA: Manifest loaded successfully
PWA: App is installable!


Complete PWA Flow (Step by Step)
=================================

Step 1: Installation & Setup

1. Install PWA Plugin:
   npm install @ducanh2912/next-pwa

2. Configure next.config.mjs:
   - Import withPWA
   - Wrap Next.js config
   - Set caching strategies
   - Configure offline fallback

3. Create manifest.json:
   - Define app name, icons, colors
   - Set display mode to "standalone"
   - Add start URL

4. Create offline.html:
   - Design offline page
   - Add theme support
   - Include app icon

5. Update Middleware:
   - Skip PWA files from middleware processing
   - Ensure direct file serving


Step 2: Build Process

When you run npm run build:

1. Next.js Build:
   - Compiles React app
   - Generates static pages
   - Optimizes assets

2. PWA Plugin Activation:
   - Scans public/ directory
   - Generates precache manifest (list of files to cache)
   - Creates sw.js with Workbox code
   - Generates workbox-*.js library file
   - Calculates hashes for cache busting

3. Service Worker Generation:
   public/
   - sw.js                    (Generated - main service worker)
   - sw.js.map                (Generated - source map, dev only)
   - workbox-1e54d6fe.js      (Generated - Workbox library)
   - workbox-1e54d6fe.js.map  (Generated - source map, dev only)
   - fallback-development.js  (Generated - dev helper)

4. Post-Build Cleanup:
   - remove-sourcemap.js runs
   - Removes source map references
   - Deletes .map files
   - Production-ready files remain


Step 3: First Visit (User's Perspective)

1. User Opens App:
   - Browser loads HTML
   - Finds <link rel="manifest" href="/manifest.json"> in HTML
   - Finds service worker registration code

2. Manifest Loading:
   - Browser fetches /manifest.json
   - Reads app metadata
   - Checks installability criteria

3. Service Worker Registration:
   - Browser downloads /sw.js
   - Registers service worker
   - Service worker enters "installing" state

4. Precaching:
   - Service worker downloads precache files
   - Stores in Cache API
   - Files include: offline.html, icons, critical assets

5. Activation:
   - Service worker becomes "active"
   - Takes control of page
   - Ready to intercept requests

6. Install Prompt (if criteria met):
   - Browser shows "Install App" button
   - User can install to home screen
   - App becomes installable


Step 4: Subsequent Visits

1. Page Request:
   - User navigates to page
   - Service worker intercepts request

2. Cache Check:
   - Service worker checks cache
   - Applies caching strategy:
     - CacheFirst: Check cache -> Use if found -> Fetch if not
     - NetworkFirst: Try network -> Cache result -> Use cache if network fails

3. Response:
   - Returns cached or fetched content
   - Updates cache if needed
   - Page loads instantly (if cached)


Step 5: Offline Scenario

1. User Goes Offline:
   - Network connection lost
   - User tries to navigate

2. Service Worker Intercepts:
   - Tries network (fails)
   - Checks cache for page

3. Two Scenarios:

   Scenario A: Page is Cached
   - Returns cached page
   - User sees content (may be slightly outdated)
   - App works normally

   Scenario B: Page Not Cached
   - Network fails
   - Cache doesn't have page
   - Service worker serves /offline.html
   - User sees "You're Offline" message

4. User Clicks Retry:
   - Page reloads
   - Service worker tries network again
   - If still offline, shows offline page again


Step 6: Service Worker Updates

1. Update Check:
   - Browser checks for new sw.js every 24 hours
   - Compares byte-by-byte with current version

2. New Version Detected:
   - Downloads new sw.js
   - New service worker enters "installing" state
   - Old service worker remains "active"

3. Installation:
   - New service worker downloads updated precache files
   - Prepares new cache

4. Activation (with skipWaiting: true):
   - New service worker activates immediately
   - Old service worker is discarded
   - New cache replaces old cache
   - Page reloads to use new service worker

5. User Experience:
   - Seamless update (if skipWaiting: true)
   - Or waits until all tabs closed (if skipWaiting: false)


Caching Strategies Explained
=============================

CacheFirst Strategy

Flow:
Request -> Check Cache -> Found? -> Return Cache
                    |
                  Not Found
                    |
              Fetch from Network
                    |
              Store in Cache
                    |
              Return Response

Best For:
- Images (PNG, JPG, SVG)
- Fonts (Google Fonts)
- Static CSS/JS files
- Icons

Why: These files rarely change, so cache is usually fresh.


NetworkFirst Strategy

Flow:
Request -> Try Network -> Success? -> Cache Response -> Return
                    |
                  Failed
                    |
              Check Cache
                    |
              Found? -> Return Cache
                    |
              Not Found -> Return Offline Page

Best For:
- HTML pages (content may change)
- API responses
- Dynamic content

Why: Content may be updated, so we want latest version, but fallback to cache if offline.


Development vs Production
==========================

Development Mode (npm run dev):

Files Generated:
- sw.js (with source maps)
- sw.js.map (for debugging)
- workbox-*.js (with source maps)
- workbox-*.js.map (for debugging)
- fallback-development.js

Behavior:
- More verbose logging
- Source maps for debugging
- Faster update checks
- Development-specific caching

Caching:
- Less aggressive caching
- NetworkFirst for most things
- Easier to see changes


Production Mode (npm run build):

Files Generated:
- sw.js (source maps removed)
- sw.js.map (deleted)
- workbox-*.js (source maps removed)
- workbox-*.js.map (deleted)
- fallback-development.js (if needed)

Behavior:
- Optimized code
- No source maps
- Production caching strategies
- Smaller file sizes

Caching:
- Aggressive caching for static assets
- Smart caching for dynamic content
- Optimized for performance


File Size & Performance
=======================

Typical File Sizes:
- sw.js: ~5-10 KB (minified)
- workbox-*.js: ~50 KB (minified)
- manifest.json: ~1 KB
- offline.html: ~3-5 KB

Total PWA Overhead: ~60-70 KB (one-time download)

Performance Benefits:
- First Load: Slightly slower (downloads service worker)
- Subsequent Loads: Much faster (served from cache)
- Offline: Works completely (no network needed)
- Bandwidth: Reduced (cached resources not re-downloaded)


Common Issues & Solutions
==========================

Issue 1: Service Worker Not Updating

Symptoms: Changes not reflecting, old version cached

Solutions:
- Clear browser cache
- Unregister service worker in DevTools
- Check skipWaiting: true in config
- Verify file hashes changed


Issue 2: Offline Page Not Showing

Symptoms: Blank page or error when offline

Solutions:
- Verify offline.html exists in public/
- Check fallbacks.document in config
- Ensure service worker is active
- Test in Incognito mode


Issue 3: Source Maps in Production

Symptoms: .map files appearing in git

Solutions:
- Run remove-sourcemap.js script
- Add *.map to .gitignore
- Verify build script includes cleanup


Issue 4: Cache Not Clearing

Symptoms: Old content showing

Solutions:
- Clear browser cache
- Unregister service worker
- Check cache expiration settings
- Verify cache names are correct


Verification Checklist
======================

Files to Verify:
- public/manifest.json exists
- public/sw.js exists (after build)
- public/offline.html exists
- public/icons/icon-192x192.png exists
- public/icons/icon-512x512.png exists
- next.config.mjs has PWA config
- src/middleware.js skips PWA files
- scripts/remove-sourcemap.js exists

Browser DevTools Checks:
- Service Worker registered (Application -> Service Workers)
- Manifest valid (Application -> Manifest)
- Cache populated (Application -> Cache Storage)
- Install prompt appears (if criteria met)
- Offline mode works (Network tab -> Offline)


Summary
=======

What We Have:

1. Service Worker (sw.js) - Handles caching and offline
2. Manifest (manifest.json) - Makes app installable
3. Offline Page (offline.html) - Shows when offline
4. Workbox Library (workbox-*.js) - Powers service worker
5. Configuration (next.config.mjs) - Sets up PWA
6. Cleanup Script (remove-sourcemap.js) - Removes dev files
7. Middleware (src/middleware.js) - Serves PWA files correctly

How It Works:

1. Build -> Generates service worker files
2. First Visit -> Registers service worker, caches files
3. Subsequent Visits -> Serves from cache (fast!)
4. Offline -> Serves cached content or offline page
5. Updates -> Automatically updates when files change

Benefits:

- Fast Loading - Cached resources load instantly
- Offline Support - Works without internet
- Installable - Can be installed like an app
- Better UX - App-like experience
- Reduced Bandwidth - Cached resources not re-downloaded

====================
